chunks: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Babawayh, from Abd al-Wahid ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abdus al-Naysaburi, from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Qutaybah, from Hamdan ibn Sulayman, from Abd al-Salam ibn Sahih al-Harawi, who said:

I said to al-Rida (peace be upon him): 'O son of the Messenger of God, it has been narrated from your forefathers (peace be upon them) that for one who has intercourse in the month of Ramadan or breaks his fast in it, there are three expiations. And it has also been narrated from them that there is one expiation. Which of the two narrations should we follow?' He said: 'We follow both. If a man has intercourse in a prohibited manner or breaks his fast in a prohibited manner in the month of Ramadan, then upon him are three expiations: freeing a slave, fasting for two consecutive months, and feeding sixty poor people, and making up that day. And if he had intercourse in a permissible manner or broke his fast in a permissible manner, then upon him is one expiation. And if he was forgetful, then there is nothing upon him.'

As for what is apart from these matters that we have enumerated, there is no expiation nor making up for any of them, because the reports that came regarding them only came as a way of dislike, and that it is preferable to avoid them. Among them is what he narrated:

key_terms.قَضَاءُ ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمِ: Making up the missed day of fasting
key_terms.كَفَّارَةٌ: Expiation or atonement for a religious violation

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the three expiations and the single expiation for breaking the fast in Ramadan according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) resolves the apparent contradiction between narrations by distinguishing between intentional violations requiring three expiations (manumission, fasting two months, feeding sixty poor) and permissible or forgetful acts requiring only one or none. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the severity of the penalty correlates with the nature of the act (haram vs. halal) and the state of mind, while other minor breaks are merely recommended to be avoided (karahat) without penalty.
